what.label: supported
what.says: The Pantheon is an ancient Roman temple, first built under Augustus and rebuilt under Hadrian; since AD 609 it has been a Catholic church.
quote: is an ancient Polytheist temple in Rome, Italy, originally built under Roman emperor Augustus (27 BC–AD 14) and reconstructed under Hadrian (117–138).
Since AD 609, it has served as the Roman Catholic Basilica of Saint Mary and the Holy Martyrs

name.label: disputed
name.says: The name means temple of all the gods, but scholars question whether it really was dedicated to all the gods; it may have been only a nickname.
quote: The simplest explanation for the name is that the Pantheon was a temple dedicated to all the gods. However, the concept of a temple dedicated to all the gods has been questioned.
this uncertainty strongly suggests that "Pantheon" (or Pantheum) was merely a nickname

inscription.label: supported
inscription.says: The inscription on the front says Marcus Agrippa, son of Lucius, made this when consul for the third time; Hadrian kept Agrippa's inscription, which is why the date is uncertain, probably around AD 126.
quote: M[arcus] Agrippa L[ucii] f[ilius] co[n]s[ul] tertium fecit, lit. 'Marcus Agrippa, son of Lucius, made [this building] when consul for the third time.'

After the original burnt down, the present building was completed by the emperor Hadrian and probably dedicated c. AD 126. Its date of construction is uncertain, because Hadrian chose to re-inscribe the new temple with Agrippa's original date inscription from the older temple.

columns.label: supported
columns.says: The granite porch columns were quarried in Egypt; each is 39 feet, 11.9 metres, tall and weighs 60 tonnes, and they came by sledge, Nile barge, sea and the Tiber.
quote: The grey granite columns used in the Pantheon's pronaos were quarried in Egypt
Each was 11.9 metres (39 ft) tall, 1.5 metres (4 ft 11 in) in diameter, and 60 tonnes
These were dragged more than 100 km (62 miles) from the mountain quarry to the river on wooden sledges. They were floated by barge down the Nile

doors.label: supported
doors.says: The big bronze doors are the original Roman doors, the oldest in Rome.
quote: The large bronze doors to the cella, measuring 4.45 metres (14.6 ft) wide by 7.53 metres (24.7 ft) high, are the oldest in Rome.
Later analysis of the fusion technique confirmed that these are the original Roman doors

dome.label: supported
dome.says: Almost two thousand years on, it is still the world's largest unreinforced concrete dome; the height to the oculus equals the diameter, 43 metres or 142 feet, so a sphere would fit inside.
quote: Almost two thousand years after it was built, the Pantheon's dome is still the world's largest unreinforced concrete dome. The height to the oculus and the diameter of the interior circle are the same, 43 metres (142 ft).
so the whole interior would fit exactly within a cube (or, a 43.3-m sphere could fit within the interior)

light.label: supported
light.says: The oculus and the door are the only natural light; the patch of light moves round the room like a reverse sundial.
quote: The oculus at the dome's apex and the entry door are the only natural sources of light in the interior. Throughout the day, light from the oculus moves around this space in a reverse sundial effect: marking time with light rather than shadow.

rain.label: supported
rain.says: The oculus was never covered; rain falls inside, and the floor slopes about 30 centimetres, 12 inches, to drains.
quote: The oculus at the top of the dome was never covered, allowing rainfall through the ceiling and onto the floor. Because of this, the interior floor is equipped with drains and has been built with an incline of about 30 centimetres (12 in) to promote water runoff.

petals.label: supported
petals.says: At Pentecost firefighters throw red rose petals down through the oculus.
quote: On Pentecost, huge quantities of red rose petals are thrown through the oculus by firefighters of the Vigili del Fuoco on the roof.

light-concrete.label: supported
light-concrete.says: The concrete gets lighter toward the top, ending in tufa and pumice, and the dome thins from 6.4 metres (21 ft) at the base to 1.2 metres (3.9 ft) at the oculus.
quote: The thickness of the dome varies from 6.4 metres (21 ft) at the base of the dome to 1.2 metres (3.9 ft) around the oculus.
then at the very top, tufa and pumice, both porous light stones

coffers.label: supported
coffers.says: The dome has five rings of 28 sunken coffers, which may once have held bronze rosettes like stars.
quote: The dome features sunken panels (coffers), in five rings of 28.
In antiquity, the coffers may have contained bronze rosettes symbolising the starry firmament.

church.label: supported
church.says: In 609 the emperor Phocas gave the building to Pope Boniface IV, who consecrated it on 13 May to St Mary and the Martyrs; becoming a church saved it from the worst of the destruction.
quote: In 609, the Byzantine emperor Phocas (who also had his namesake column constructed nearby) gave the building to Pope Boniface IV, who converted it into a Christian church and consecrated it to St. Mary and the Martyrs on 13 May 609
The building's consecration as a church saved it from the abandonment, destruction, and the worst of the spoliation that befell the majority of ancient Rome's buildings during the Early Middle Ages.

constans.label: supported
constans.says: In 663 the emperor Constans II stripped the bronze roof tiles and shipped them to Constantinople.
quote: Paul the Deacon records the spoliation of the building by the Emperor Constans II, who visited Rome in July 663
and he took away from there the bronze tiles and sent them with all the other ornaments to Constantinople.

barberini.label: disputed
barberini.says: Pope Urban VIII melted the porch's bronze trusses; it is said they went into Bernini's canopy at St Peter's, but the pope's accounts show about 90% went into cannon. A satirist quipped: what the barbarians did not do, the Barberini did.
quote: most controversially the removal and melting down of the massive bronze trusses above the portico

It is also said that the bronze was used by Bernini in creating his famous baldachin above the high altar of St. Peter's Basilica, though the archaeologist Carlo Fea discovered from the Pope's accounts that about 90% of the bronze was used for the cannon, and that the bronze for the baldachin came from Venice.
("What the barbarians did not do the Barberinis [Urban VIII's family name] did")

raphael.label: supported
raphael.says: The painter Raphael is buried here, in the third niche on the left side, past the tomb of King Umberto I; his fiancée Maria Bibbiena, who died before they could marry, lies to the right.
quote: On the first niche to the left of the entrance
The tomb of King Umberto I and his wife Margherita di Savoia is in the next chapel.
The third niche holds the mortal remains
of the great artist Raphael. His fiancée, Maria Bibbiena is buried to the right of his sarcophagus; she died before they could marry.

epitaph.label: supported
epitaph.says: Raphael's epitaph, by Pietro Bembo, says Nature feared to be outdone by him while he lived, and to die when he died.
quote: meaning "Here lies Raphael, by whom the great mother of all things (Nature) feared to be overcome while he was living, and while he was dying, herself to die". The epigraph was written by Pietro Bembo.

kings.label: supported
kings.says: Two kings of Italy, Victor Emmanuel II and Umberto I, are buried here.
quote: two monarchs of the Kingdom of Italy were buried in the Pantheon; Vittorio Emanuele II and Umberto I

charles.label: legend
charles.says: Legend says that when Emperor Charles V climbed the dome in 1536, his young guide felt an urge to push him through the oculus in revenge for the Sack of Rome.
quote: In April 1536, after the Conquest of Tunis, the emperor visited Rome in a triumphal procession that included a visit to the Pantheon. According to legend, Charles wanted to climb the dome to peer down through the oculus. His guide, the keeper's son, recounts feeling a sudden urge to push the emperor over the edge of the opening as revenge for the city's devastation.

church-now.label: supported
church-now.says: It is still a working church; visitors are asked to keep an appropriate deference, and Mass is said on Sundays.
quote: The Pantheon is in use as a Catholic church, and as such, visitors are asked to keep an appropriate level of deference. Masses are celebrated there on Sundays and holy days of obligation.

parts.name: The porch
parts.stand: Stand in the square in front, where you can see the whole porch of columns and the words carved above them.

paras.t: This is the Pantheon, a Roman temple first built under Augustus and rebuilt under Hadrian. Since AD 609 it has been a church, and that's why it's still standing.

Read the big letters above the columns. They say Marcus Agrippa, son of Lucius, made this when consul for the third time. But Agrippa's temple burned. This building is Hadrian's, probably dedicated around AD 126. Hadrian simply kept the old inscription, which is why the date is uncertain.
The name means temple of all the gods, though scholars aren't sure it ever really was one; it may have been just a nickname.
Those granite columns came from Egypt. Each is 39 feet tall and weighs 60 tonnes. They were dragged on sledges to the Nile, floated down by barge, shipped across the sea, and pulled up the Tiber.
Now the doors as you go in. These bronze doors are the originals, the oldest doors in Rome.

parts.name: Under the dome
parts.stand: Go in and stand in the middle of the floor, under the round opening, and look straight up.

paras.t: Look up. Almost two thousand years old, this is still the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world. From the floor to the opening is about 142 feet, 43 meters, exactly the width of the room, so a giant ball would fit inside perfectly.
That opening, the oculus, has never had glass. It and the door are the only natural light. Look for the circle of sunlight; through the day it travels round the room like a sundial in reverse.
And when it rains, it rains inside. Look down: the floor slopes about 12 inches toward drains. On Pentecost, firefighters on the roof pour red rose petals through the oculus.

How does it stay up? The concrete gets lighter as it rises, ending in light volcanic stone near the top, and the shell thins from 21 feet at the base to about 4 feet at the rim of the opening. Count the sunken squares, the coffers: five rings of 28. They may once have held bronze rosettes, like stars.
In 609 the emperor gave this building to Pope Boniface IV, who dedicated it on May 13 to Saint Mary and the Martyrs. Becoming a church saved it, when most of ancient Rome was being torn apart.
Even so, it was robbed. In 663 the emperor Constans II stripped the bronze roof tiles and shipped them off to Constantinople.

Later, Pope Urban VIII melted down the bronze beams of the porch. People said it went into Bernini's canopy at Saint Peter's, but his accounts show about 90 percent went into cannon, so that story is probably wrong. A Roman wit summed it up: what the barbarians did not do, the Barberini did. Barberini was the pope's family name.
It's still a working church, with Mass on Sundays, so keep your voice low.

parts.name: Raphael's tomb
parts.stand: From the entrance, walk round to your left until you are just past the tomb of King Umberto; Raphael is in the next niche.

paras.t: Here lies the great painter Raphael. Beside him, to the right, is Maria Bibbiena, his fiancée, who died before they could marry.
His epitaph was written by the poet Pietro Bembo. It says that while Raphael lived, Nature feared he would outdo her, and when he died, she feared she would die with him.
Two kings of Italy are buried here too, Victor Emmanuel II and Umberto I.

There's a legend about this dome. In 1536 the emperor Charles V, whose armies had sacked Rome, wanted to climb up and look down through the oculus. His guide, the keeper's son, later said he felt a sudden urge to push him in.

parts.name: Closing
parts.stand: On your way out, stop in the doorway and look back up at the light.

paras.t: Romans built this for their gods. Christians have prayed in it for over fourteen centuries. And the rain still comes straight in through the roof, as it always has. Stand here a moment and let the sky in.
